general.reason: The paper explicitly states 'All experiments are conducted in simulation using a randomized 2D deformable sheet model' with 'Laplacian relaxation' and acknowledges future work to 'validate on real tissue data,' confirming the simulation is far from realistic surgical tissue and generalization claims are unvalidated.

evidence.claim: The experimental setup uses an overly simplified 2D cloth simulation that is not representative of real surgical tissue retraction, making the generalization of results to surgery unjustified.
evidence.excerpt: The simulation uses a 2D cloth-like sheet with a regular 30×30 grid and Laplacian relaxation. This is a reasonable toy environment, but it is quite far from realistic surgical tissue deformation. Tissue is often nonuniform, anisotropic, constrained by attachments, subject to contact/friction, and observed through highly structured occlusions rather than random visible vertices.

judge_panel.reason: The paper explicitly states 'All experiments are conducted in simulation using a randomized 2D deformable sheet model' with 'Laplacian relaxation' and acknowledges future work to 'validate on real tissue data,' confirming the simulation is far from realistic surgical tissue and generalization claims are unvalidated.

The paper evaluates only in a simplified simulator: it uses a “2D deformable sheet simulation,” with the tissue “discretized on a regular 30×30 grid of vertices” and “Deformation uses Laplacian relaxation [13].” The paper itself says “in ongoing and future work, we plan to validate on real tissue data,” so it does not justify generalization to real surgery from this setup alone.

The paper explicitly states it uses a "randomized 2D deformable sheet model" with a "regular 30x30 grid" and "Laplacian relaxation," confirming the reviewer's concern about the simplified experimental setup.

judge_panel.reason: The paper reports only one p-value (p=0.835 for oracle sampling budget) and provides means and success rates without standard deviations, confidence intervals, or paired test results comparing the learned estimator to oracle and baseline in the main results.

Although the paper says “Metrics include exposure improvement, success rate, and statistical significance measured using paired and independent t-tests,” the only explicit test result reported is “An independent t-test between nsamples = 200 and 2000 yields p = 0.835.” For the main learned-vs-oracle comparisons, it reports means and success rates but no standard deviations/confidence intervals or p-values, despite concluding “statistically equivalent to a full-state oracle.”

The paper states that "statistical significance measured using paired and independent t-tests" is used, but only reports a single p-value (p = 0.835) in Section III.C, omitting standard deviations, confidence intervals, and p-values for the main comparisons.

The conclusion claims “planning-sufficient learned representations can replace expensive physical simulation,” but the method still uses model-based action evaluation: “Actions are selected by sampling 200 candidate pulls and choosing the one that maximizes predicted exposure under the estimated state,” and “Deformation in response to actions is modeled using a diffusion-based relaxation process [11].” The paper does not clearly explain what simulation is actually being replaced.

The conclusion claims the method can "replace expensive physical simulation," yet Section II.C notes the planner chooses actions that "maximize predicted exposure under the estimated state," which seemingly implies relying on simulation for forward rollouts.

general.reason: The paper states 'the system observes only 40 of 900 vertices (4.4%), resampled at random each time' with 'Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ=0.02,' which assumes known vertex indices sampled uniformly—an unrealistic assumption compared to real surgical perception from images or point clouds with registration uncertainty.

evidence.claim: The observation model assumes known mesh vertex indices sampled uniformly at random, which is unrealistic compared to practical surgical perception scenarios.
evidence.excerpt: The method assumes that 40 vertex indices and their noisy coordinates are available, with vertices sampled uniformly at random. In real surgical perception, observations are not random known mesh vertices. Instead, observations come from images or point clouds with occlusions, registration uncertainty, missing regions, specularities, and correspondence ambiguity.

judge_panel.reason: The paper states 'the system observes only 40 of 900 vertices (4.4%), resampled at random each time' with 'Gaussian noise with standard deviation σ=0.02,' which assumes known vertex indices sampled uniformly—an unrealistic assumption compared to real surgical perception from images or point clouds with registration uncertainty.

The paper explicitly assumes idealized correspondence information: “the system observes only 40 of 900 vertices (4.4%), resampled at random each time” and “The network takes as input the observed vertex coordinates and their indices.” It does not model the more realistic image/point-cloud observation ambiguities raised in the flag.

The paper explicitly assumes access to vertex correspondence, noting that "the network takes as input the observed vertex coordinates and their indices," and that vertices are "resampled at random each time," which justifies the reviewer's concern regarding real-world applicability.
